lesson_title: Day 2 Daily Quiz: Review of Day 1

metadata.note: Instructor-only 08:45 quiz on day 1; every question traces to a visible slide.

questions.question_stem: A hand-built Bitcoin transaction spends one 0.5 BTC input and pays 0.2 BTC to a merchant, with no change output. What happens to the other 0.3 BTC?
questions.correct_answer: It becomes the fee: the fee is whatever the inputs hold that the outputs do not pay out, and the miner keeps it.
incorrect_answers: It stays in the original output, which remains unspent because the transaction only used part of that coin.
It returns to the paying address automatically, since nodes add a change output when none is listed there.
Nodes reject the transaction, because a valid payment must list a fee field that matches the outputs exactly.
questions.explanation: A Bitcoin transaction has no fee field. Inputs are spent whole, so any value the outputs leave out goes to the miner; leaving out the change output turns the change into the fee.

specific_source.reading: The fee is the leftover, written nowhere

questions.question_stem: An explorer page for a Bitcoin payment shows a fee of 0.0005 BTC and tags the paying address 'Exchange'. How should an analyst treat these two items?
questions.correct_answer: The fee is worked out from earlier amounts; the tag is the explorer operator's own label, a Low-confidence lead.
incorrect_answers: Both come straight from the chain, so the fee and the tag can each be quoted as recorded facts in a report.
The tag comes from the chain but the fee is the explorer's estimate, so only the tag can be quoted as a fact.
The fee is stored in the transaction as a field, while the tag is the node's own record of who owns the address shown.
questions.explanation: The transaction's input names an earlier output but not its amount, so the explorer derives the fee. A tag is whoever runs the explorer's claim: a lead, not a fact.

specific_source.reading: An explorer is a node's record, plus extras

questions.question_stem: An explorer shows a suspect's payment as 'unconfirmed'. An agent wants the report to say the suspect paid. What is the best response?
questions.correct_answer: Say it was seen, not settled: it waits in nodes' memory and may fade away if no miner ever includes it.
incorrect_answers: Report it as paid, since every node has checked the signature and the payment cannot be reversed.
Report it as paid once the explorer's tag confirms which exchange the sender is known to use.
Report it as failed, because a payment missing from the blockchain was rejected by the network.
questions.explanation: Unconfirmed transactions sit in each node's memory pool, which is lost when a node restarts; one that is never mined fades away. Unconfirmed means seen, not settled.

specific_source.reading: Unconfirmed is not paid: it can still vanish

questions.question_stem: A colleague applies Bitcoin change-output tracing, looking for a returned remainder, to a transfer on Ethereum. Why does the clue not carry over?
questions.correct_answer: Account-model chains move value from one balance to another and have no change outputs, so no clue exists.
incorrect_answers: Ethereum transfers hide the sender, so there is no paying address to which any change could return.
Ethereum spends whole coins like Bitcoin but pads each one with change, so every output looks alike on the page.
The course chain keeps no record of balances, so a returned remainder cannot be told from the fee.
questions.explanation: Bitcoin keeps unspent outputs, so a payment spends whole outputs and makes change. Ethereum and the course chain keep accounts, so the change-output heuristic does not apply.

specific_source.reading: Bitcoin keeps no balances, only unspent coins

questions.question_stem: A transaction was signed with the key that controls address X. Which sentence does the signature itself support in a report?
questions.correct_answer: The transaction was signed with the key controlling address X; who held that key needs other evidence.
incorrect_answers: Smith, the owner of address X, approved this transaction, because only the owner can produce the signature.
The holder of the key understood and intended this transfer, because the signature covers its exact bytes.
One person decided to send the funds, since a valid signature shows a single human approved the payment.
questions.explanation: A signature proves the key approved these exact bytes. Keys can be stolen, shared or held by a service, so naming a person or showing intent takes other evidence.

specific_source.reading: A signature authorizes; it doesn't identify

questions.question_stem: An Ethereum transaction carries no sender field, yet an explorer shows a 'From' address. Why can a sender not simply type in someone else's address?
questions.correct_answer: Every node recovers the public key from the signature and hashes it into the address, so a forged sender fails.
incorrect_answers: The public key travels beside the signature, as in a Bitcoin input, and nodes compare it with the typed sender.
Ethereum nodes check the typed sender against a registry of known addresses and refuse any unlisted one.
The explorer looks the sender up in exchange customer records and rejects any address that is not registered there.
questions.explanation: The transaction carries a signature (v, r, s). From it and the transaction hash, any node recovers the public key and hashes it to the address, so the From field is computed, not sent.

specific_source.reading: Ethereum works out the sender from the signature

questions.question_stem: The same 20 bytes appear in an Ethereum address beginning 0x2a26 and in a Tron address beginning T. What may an analyst conclude?
questions.correct_answer: One key made both, so one controller is likely: a lead to confirm, not a finding alone.
incorrect_answers: Nothing, because Tron uses SHA-256 and Ethereum uses Keccak-256, so those matches are chance.
Both belong to one exchange, because the 41 prefix marks an address that a service runs.
The funds moved between chains, because identical bytes mean one transaction crossed a bridge.
questions.explanation: Tron derives its address as Ethereum does, then adds a 0x41 byte and Base58Check encoding. Matching bytes mean the same key, which is a lead for the same controller.

specific_source.reading: A Tron address is an Ethereum address plus 41

questions.question_stem: Coins are drained from a wallet whose keys came from a generator seeded with only 32 bits. What does the chain show, and why was the theft possible?
questions.correct_answer: An ordinary valid signed transaction; attackers recreated the keys by trying every seed, and secp256k1 itself stayed unbroken.
incorrect_answers: A forged signature, because attackers broke secp256k1 by solving the discrete logarithm problem from the public key alone on the chain.
An invalid transaction that nodes still accepted, because weak keys let the sender skip the signature check entirely.
A flagged theft, because the chain marks transactions signed by weak keys and lets the owner revoke that key right away, too.
questions.explanation: No one has broken secp256k1. With a 32-bit seed, attackers could regenerate the keys (Milk Sad, 2023). On chain the theft looks like any signed transaction, and a stolen key cannot be revoked.

specific_source.reading: Keys fail through people and bad randomness

questions.question_stem: A briefing says the blockchain is 'immutable: it can never change'. What is the more accurate wording for a report?
questions.correct_answer: Tamper-evident: an edit to an old entry shows, but the newest entries can change until consensus makes them final.
incorrect_answers: Fully immutable: hash-linking and replication make every entry, even the newest block, impossible to reorder.
Tamper-evident only because one trusted operator holds the master copy and checks each new entry for edits.
Editable by anyone: each copy is independent, so a party that rewrites its own copy changes the shared record.
questions.explanation: Hash-chaining makes a changed old entry break every later link, and replication means one rewritten copy changes nothing. Only consensus protects the newest entries, and that takes time.

questions.question_stem: On Bitcoin, a payment with one confirmation drops out of its block, then appears in a later block. No attack is suspected. What most likely happened?
questions.correct_answer: Two miners found valid blocks nearly together; the other block went stale and its payments went back to the mempool.
incorrect_answers: A majority attacker has rewritten the block, since any reordering of recent blocks is proof of a double spend by an attacker.
The explorer deleted the payment because its mempool restarted, and a miner then repeated the old signature.
The block was edited by its miner, whose hash link then updated every later block to match the change made.
questions.explanation: Network delay lets two valid blocks compete; nodes follow the chain with the most work and the loser is stale. Its transactions return to the mempool, so cite the block hash as well as the height.

specific_source.reading: A stale block is routine, not an attack

questions.question_stem: A memo must say when an Ethereum transfer and a Bitcoin payment count as 'final'. Which pairing is correct?
questions.correct_answer: Bitcoin never declares finality; Ethereum finalizes a checkpoint once two-thirds of the staked ETH votes for it.
incorrect_answers: Both are final once included in a block, because the block's miner or validator has signed that block.
Bitcoin is final after six confirmations as a rule, while Ethereum is final once its next block of 12 seconds is built.
Bitcoin finalizes by a vote of mining power, while Ethereum is final at once after six confirmations.
questions.explanation: Proof of work finalizes gradually: each block makes reversal harder, and six is a convention. Ethereum's proof of stake finalizes a checkpoint when votes from two-thirds of staked ETH arrive (about 15 minutes).

specific_source.reading: Each chain puts a different number on "final"

questions.question_stem: A transaction has sat unconfirmed for hours and an agent says it is being censored. What should the analyst write?
questions.correct_answer: A low fee, a miner exclusion or a relay failure could each explain it, and they look alike.
incorrect_answers: Censorship is the likely cause, because every node shares one mempool and a stuck item was refused.
A fault, not censorship, since miners pick transactions only by arrival time and never by fee.
Congestion is certain, because a transaction paying the minimum fee must always wait a long time.
questions.explanation: There is no single mempool, and miners choose by fee per byte. A stuck transaction has at least three explanations and only one is censorship, so name the alternatives you cannot rule out.

specific_source.reading: Delay may mean congestion, not censorship
